Delay: 7 days of notice plus my estimate of two weeks for containment, removal and air clearance.

eventCatalog.name: The block is in a historic district
eventCatalog.text: Your storefront is in a historic district. The sign, the awning and the new door need a Landmarks permit before the Buildings permit can be issued.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Address inside a designated historic district (public map of the Landmarks Preservation Commission)
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Applies to every storefront in a historic district; 95% of approvals are issued by staff without a hearing (LPC, April 2025)
eventCatalog.note: Staff permit within 10 business days (FasTrack) or 15 business days for a complete application = up to 21 calendar days. Fee $95 for the first $25,000 of work plus $5 per $1,000: $320 on a $70,000 job. A design that needs a Commission hearing takes months.

eventCatalog.name: The building has no Certificate of Occupancy
eventCatalog.text: The building is older than 1938 and has no Certificate of Occupancy on file. Before permits, the Buildings Department must issue a Letter of No Objection for a cafe.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Building built or altered before 1938 with no Certificate of Occupancy in Buildings Department records
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Common in older low-rise buildings; no count found
eventCatalog.note: One architecture firm: at least one month for a clear case. If the letter is refused the use is not legal and the lease is worthless without the cancellation clause.

eventCatalog.name: The landlord's unpaid fines block your permit
eventCatalog.text: The building owes the city more than $25,000 in unpaid penalties. The permit system refuses your application until you prove you are only a tenant.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Property flagged for arrears or excessive violations in the Buildings Department property profile (Local Law 160 of 2017, Local Law 104 of 2019)
eventCatalog.realFrequency: No count found; the flag is visible in the public property profile before signing
eventCatalog.note: Local Law 160 of 2017: permits are denied where covered arrears on the property or its owners exceed $25,000 (threshold from a compliance-service summary); an exception lets the commissioner issue a permit for a part of the property occupied by a tenant who is not an owner and not responsible for the arrears. 14 days is my estimate for documenting the exception.

eventCatalog.name: An inspector tapes a Stop Work Order to the door
eventCatalog.text: Someone called 311 about the dumpster and the noise. The inspector found no permit on the wall. All work stops today.
eventCatalog.realSignal: A 311 construction complaint on a site with no posted permit
eventCatalog.realFrequency: DOB publishes enforcement bulletins every month; one listed site drew $188,750 in penalties for unpermitted work against an active Stop Work Order
eventCatalog.note: Penalty for work without a permit: 21 x the permit fee, minimum $6,000, maximum $15,000. Delay: drawings (21 days) + approval (about 21 days) + a few days to rescind the order = 45 days, during which rent runs ($9,000 at $6,000 a month).

eventCatalog.name: The plumbing fails inspection
eventCatalog.text: The inspector asks which licensed plumber did the work. Nobody did. The lines are opened up and redone.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Plumbing or electrical work with no licensed firm on the filing
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Individual cases reported: a plumber working without a supervising master plumber was fined $5,000 in 2022
eventCatalog.note: Redo by licensed firms at the full price the handyman undercut ($12,000, my estimate of the licensed plumbing and electrical share of a $70,000 job) plus the $5,000 penalty of the reported case; 14 days is my estimate.

eventCatalog.name: The city cuts small-business red tape
eventCatalog.text: City Hall announces more than 50 reforms for small businesses: a free project manager for anyone opening, one permit instead of two for frozen desserts, lower fines for three food-safety violations.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Mayoral executive orders and Small Business Services announcements (Executive Order 11 of January 14, 2026; Executive Order 18 and "OPEN for Small Business" of July 20, 2026)
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Two packages in 2026; the NYC Hospitality Alliance called the July one limited
eventCatalog.note: Real: 50+ reforms for about 180,000 small businesses, 25 of them for food businesses; frozen dessert permit eliminated; three food-safety fines cut from $600 to $500 (500/600 = 0.83). The 10% shorter permit wait from the project manager is a design value: no measured effect exists yet.

eventCatalog.name: Waiting for the gas to be turned on
eventCatalog.text: The piping is in and tested, but the utility has not come to set the meter. Without gas the water heater and the oven are dead.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Utility gas service request pending after the Buildings Department gas authorization
eventCatalog.realFrequency: State Senate survey of city restaurants (2017): only 17% got service on time, 69% waited at least 30 days, the average was about 68 days, some waited up to a year; a Lower East Side restaurant opened with salads after seven months
eventCatalog.note: The survey is from 2017; no newer measurement was found. The delay bites only if gas is on the critical path: an all-electric coffee shop skips it entirely. Page opened (State Senate report, September 2017): average wait about 68 days, majority at least 30 days, one respondent over a year; total reported losses almost $2.2 million, over $140,000 per business.

eventCatalog.name: The gas to the building is shut off
eventCatalog.text: A routine utility inspection found a leak in the building's piping. Gas is off for every tenant until the landlord's plumber repairs it and the city passes it.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Utility leak finding on the building's gas piping (periodic inspections under Local Law 152)
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Reported every year: a Hell's Kitchen restaurant cooked without gas for about six weeks in spring 2026; Riverdale businesses went months without gas in 2024
eventCatalog.note: Duration from the 2026 case (six weeks and counting). The quality and capacity effects are design values for a cafe that heats water and food with gas.

eventCatalog.name: The panel cannot carry the equipment
eventCatalog.text: The electrician adds up the espresso machine, the ice machine, the fridges and the air conditioning. The old panel is too small, and a bigger service needs Con Edison.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Existing electrical service of the space against the equipment load (visible on a walk-through with an electrician)
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Listed by NYC contractors as one of the usual surprises in old buildings, with old plumbing and grease-trap sizing; no rate found
eventCatalog.note: Two to six weeks of Con Edison coordination (contractor guides): 28 days is the midpoint. If the street side must be upgraded the utility's own 2021 sheet says 6 to 24 months. $9,000 is the weak estimate of electrical_service_upgrade.

eventCatalog.name: Con Edison asks for a deposit
eventCatalog.text: Your business has no payment history. The utility wants a security deposit before it opens the account.
eventCatalog.realSignal: New non-residential account with no billing history
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Standard for new business accounts
eventCatalog.note: Cap: two times the average monthly bill; $800 of electricity x 2 = $1,600. A buyer of an operating shop cannot keep the seller's account and faces the same deposit.

eventCatalog.name: The walls are opened and the surprises come out
eventCatalog.text: Behind the old counter: rotted subfloor, a drain that goes nowhere, wiring from another century. None of it was in the bid.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Age and prior use of the space; none of it visible without opening walls
eventCatalog.realFrequency: NYC contractors list undersized electrical, old plumbing, grease-trap sizing and code-triggered upgrades as the typical surprises; a Brooklyn cafe owner: "so many unforeseen costs and delays in build-out" (Barista Magazine)
eventCatalog.note: 12% is inside the contingency contractors recommend (10-15% of hard costs): with a 15% reserve the event is absorbed; with 5% the difference is paid at the change-order premium of 15-30%. 14 days is my estimate.

eventCatalog.name: Change orders pile up
eventCatalog.text: The low bid left things out. Every missing item comes back as a change order, priced by a contractor who knows you cannot switch now.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Bid well below the others; scope gaps in the contract
eventCatalog.realFrequency: A contractor guide: change orders happen on almost every restaurant build; unplanned ones cost a 15-30% premium
eventCatalog.note: Design values: the 12% saved on the low bid is more than returned as 20% of extras. One trade article cites an average restaurant renovation overrun of 34% without naming a study.

eventCatalog.name: A buckling wall stops the job
eventCatalog.text: The crew uncovers a wall that is bowing. Work stops until an engineer and the landlord agree who fixes the building.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Structural condition of an old building, found only during demolition
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Rare but real: the owners of the relaunched Le Figaro Cafe sued their landlord in 2022 after permit delays and then a buckling interior wall stopped their contractors, claiming about $2 million in losses
eventCatalog.note: 120 days is a design value for "months" in the reported case. Structure is the landlord's under most leases, but the tenant's rent clock runs unless the lease says otherwise.

eventCatalog.name: A worker falls from a ladder on your job
eventCatalog.text: A laborer on the cheap crew fell while hanging the ceiling. His lawyer names the building owner, the contractor and you: the tenant who ordered the work.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Contractor with no liability insurance or no workers' compensation on a job the tenant contracted
eventCatalog.realFrequency: No rate found. The legal rule is firm: under Labor Law §240(1) owners are absolutely liable, and courts treat a tenant who contracted for the work as an owner (Sanatass v. Consolidated Investing, Court of Appeals 2008; Otero v. 635 Owner LLC)
eventCatalog.note: The $25,000 is a design value standing for a deductible and legal costs; real scaffold-law judgments run far higher and are the reason NYC contractors' insurance is expensive. An insured contractor who names the tenant on the certificate removes the event.

eventCatalog.name: Contractors raise their prices
eventCatalog.text: This year's cost guides are out: fitting out a store in New York costs 7% more than last year.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Cushman & Wakefield Retail Fit-Out Cost Guide, published each March: New York in-line retail $181 per sq ft in 2026, up 7.0%
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Yearly; NYC +7.0% in 2026 against +1.4% nationally
eventCatalog.note: Applies to build-out contracts signed after the announcement. The guide measures plain retail fit-outs, not food service.

eventCatalog.name: The espresso machine costs 15% more
eventCatalog.text: The United States taxes European goods at 15%. Your Italian machine and grinders are on the list.
eventCatalog.realSignal: US tariff rate on goods from the European Union (15% since late July 2025)
eventCatalog.realFrequency: In force since mid-2025; makers and dealers split on how much they pass through
eventCatalog.note: Upper bound: full pass-through on the two-group machine ($7,600 x 0.15 = $1,140) and the grinders. Buying a shop with its equipment, or used gear already in the country, avoids it.

eventCatalog.name: The contractor's invoice comes with sales tax
eventCatalog.text: The final invoice adds 8.875% sales tax. Your lease never said the improvements belong to the landlord, so the state treats the job as a taxable installation.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Lease silent on ownership of improvements; no Form ST-124 given to the contractor
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Depends on the lease; the Tax Department presumes tenant installations are temporary
eventCatalog.note: 8.875% on the labor-and-markup 60% of the bill = 5.3% of the build-out ($3,728 on $70,000). The 60% share is my assumption.

eventCatalog.name: The Health inspector cannot inspect a construction site
eventCatalog.text: You asked for the pre-permit inspection to open early. It needs all construction finished and no food on the premises. The punch list is not done.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Pre-permit inspection requested before construction is complete
eventCatalog.realFrequency: A standing rule (NYC311): all construction must be complete and no food of any kind may be on site
eventCatalog.note: The fallback is the 22-day rule: a new applicant may open on the 22nd day after applying even with no inspection. 7 days is my estimate for rebooking.

eventCatalog.name: The first graded inspection, unannounced
eventCatalog.text: An inspector walks in during the morning rush. Thirteen points or fewer is an A in the window. Fourteen or more means "Grade Pending" and a second visit in about a month.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Initial inspection of a new permit holder; score computed from the violations actually present

effects.note: only if the score is 14 or more

eventCatalog.realFrequency: Every new restaurant; 0-13 points is an A at once, 14 or more is ungraded with a re-inspection about a month later
eventCatalog.note: No dice: the score is the sum of points for the violations the shop really has (extra.inspectionPoints in the pack). The $100 consultative inspection, available once food service has begun, lets the owner clear them first. The reputation effect is a design value.

eventCatalog.name: The state claims the seller's unpaid sales tax
eventCatalog.text: Five days after your bulk-sale notice, the Tax Department answers with a Notice of Claim. The seller owes sales tax. The purchase money must sit in escrow until the state names the amount.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Seller's sales-tax account with the state at the time of the bulk-sale notice (Form AU-196.2 instead of a release)
eventCatalog.realFrequency: No rate published; the Division of Tax Appeals has a steady docket of deli and restaurant buyers disputing these claims (Bernard & Varecha Deli; 1646 Kosher Deli; St. James Colonial Deli)
eventCatalog.note: Bulletin TB-ST-70: answer within 5 business days of the notice; within 90 days of receipt the Department must state the amount; the buyer pays the state from escrow up to the higher of price or fair market value and the rest to the seller. 90 days is the legal outer limit, used as the delay. The buyer loses time, not money.

eventCatalog.name: A tax bill arrives for the previous owner's sales
eventCatalog.text: A notice from the Tax Department: the shop's previous owner under-reported sales for three years. No bulk-sale notice was filed, so the debt is now yours.
eventCatalog.realSignal: State sales-tax audit of the seller after a purchase closed with no Form AU-196.10

effects.note: the listing's hidden debt, capped at the purchase price

eventCatalog.realFrequency: Documented in Tax Appeals determinations and trade press ("Buying a restaurant? Watch out for the seller's sales tax liabilities", Total Food Service)
eventCatalog.note: Liability cap: the higher of the purchase price or the fair market value of the assets (TB-ST-70). The $30,000 is a design example: three years of 5% under-reported sales on $612,000 a year x 8.875% = $8,150 of tax, with penalty and interest and a typical audit mark-up it can reach several times that. Each listing should carry its own hidden figure.

eventCatalog.name: The sales were never what the listing said
eventCatalog.text: The seller swore the shop did a third more in cash than the books showed. Your first month matches the books, not the story.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Gap between the listing's stated sales and the register reports, bank deposits and filed sales-tax returns
eventCatalog.realFrequency: A standing warning from business brokers: unrecorded-cash claims are the first of the "untruths told to buyers"; the check is 24 months of register data against bank deposits
eventCatalog.note: The 20% gap is a design value. A price set at 2.0 times overstated earnings overpays by the same proportion: on the reference shop, 20% of $233,000 = $46,600.

eventCatalog.name: The espresso machine belongs to a lender
eventCatalog.text: A finance company writes: the machine and the grinders were leased, and the seller stopped paying. Pay off the balance or they collect the equipment.
eventCatalog.realSignal: UCC financing statement or equipment lease on the seller's assets (public lien search)
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Listed among the red flags of coffee-shop purchases: "espresso equipment under financing lien that the seller cannot release at closing"
eventCatalog.note: The $6,000 payoff is a design value: about the remaining half of a financed $9,700 machine-and-grinder set plus fees.

eventCatalog.name: Closed for 22 days after the handover
eventCatalog.text: The seller's Health permit ended with the sale and yours is not issued yet. The law lets you open on the 22nd day after you applied, and you applied today.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Date of the buyer's own permit application against the closing date
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Applies to every sale: Health Code §5.11 voids a permit on transfer
eventCatalog.note: 22 days of the reference month: 22/30 x ($51,000 sales - $13,260 cost of goods) = $27,700 of margin lost while rent and wages run.

eventCatalog.name: The seller left unpaid Health Department fines
eventCatalog.text: Your permit application is on hold: the records show violations and penalties the previous owner never settled. The city wants proof that you bought the shop at arm's length.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Outstanding violations or unpaid penalties of the seller in Health Department and hearing-office records
eventCatalog.realFrequency: No count found; the rule is in Health Code Article 5
eventCatalog.note: Health Code Article 5, seen in extract (sentence cut off): the Commissioner shall not issue a new permit based on a sale or change of ownership where records show outstanding uncorrected violations or unpaid penalties, with an exception when the applicant proves an arm's-length sale; a sale to a relative or a related company is presumed not to be one. 14 days is my estimate for the paperwork. The full text of the subsection was not read.

eventCatalog.name: You inherit the seller's unemployment-insurance record
eventCatalog.text: The Labor Department moved the previous owner's account to you. He laid off staff twice; your contribution rate is recalculated from the day you took over.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Seller's unemployment-insurance experience account balance at transfer (NY Labor Law §581)
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Automatic on any transfer of all or part of a business; courts have refused to let a buyer escape a poor rating by not reporting the purchase
eventCatalog.note: Rule from the Labor Department page. The size is a design value: +2 percentage points on the first $17,600 of each worker's wages (2026 wage base), about $350 a worker a year. A good record can equally lower the rate below the new-employer 4.1%. Page opened (NYS Department of Labor): "the buyer takes on all prior unemployment insurance experience, including but not limited to the previous experience rating account balance, and unemployment charges for former employees"; the rate "will be determined or redetermined as of the date of the transfer".

eventCatalog.name: The landlord names a price for consent
eventCatalog.text: The lease needs the landlord's consent to an assignment. The landlord will consent: with a new guaranty, a bigger deposit and the rent brought up to market.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Assignment clause of the seller's lease; inherited rent against market rent
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Routine. Where consent may not be unreasonably withheld the landlord must show a reasonable ground (F&F Restaurant v. Wells, Goode, Court of Appeals 1984); many leases give the landlord a right to take the space back instead
eventCatalog.note: The 10% rent step and two extra months of deposit are design values. A recapture clause can end the deal outright; the seller stays liable on the lease after assignment unless released.

eventCatalog.name: Three years left on the lease you bought
eventCatalog.text: The price looked low because the lease was short. It ends in three years, and a commercial tenant in New York has no right to renew.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Years remaining on the assigned lease (stated in the listing or the lease)
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Stated in listings: one Queens diner was offered at $275,000 with four years left at $5,100 a month; a Manhattan store advertised 12 years remaining as a selling point
eventCatalog.note: The 25% jump at renewal is a design value. Holdover without a renewal costs 150-200% of rent. Brokers: a coffee shop that loses its lease typically cannot relocate and survive.

eventCatalog.name: The regulars notice the new owner
eventCatalog.text: New name on the door, new beans, strangers behind the counter. Some regulars try you once and go back to the place around the corner.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Changes made in the first month after a purchase
eventCatalog.realFrequency: No statistic; advisers on small-business sales name owner dependence as a main driver of post-sale regret
eventCatalog.note: Design values: 0.6 / 0.9 = 0.67 of the regulars kept by a quiet handover (levers takeover_transition).

eventCatalog.name: The machine you bought with the shop dies
eventCatalog.text: The espresso machine came with the business and with its years. It fails in the morning rush, months after the seller's promises ended.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Age of the equipment at purchase against its service life (seven years for an espresso machine in the pack)
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Deterministic in the game: the item fails when its remaining life (lifespanMonths minus age) runs out
eventCatalog.note: Replacement price $7,600 and 84-month life are the pack's own figures for the two-group machine. The listing states the equipment age; the full review turns it into a price reduction.

eventCatalog.name: The bank wants 10% of your own money
eventCatalog.text: You planned to buy the shop on a loan and a seller note. The SBA rules require a tenth of the whole project from you, and a seller note counts only if the seller waits ten years to be paid.
eventCatalog.realSignal: SBA Standard Operating Procedure 50 10 8 (June 1, 2025) and 50 10 8.1 (applications from October 1, 2026)
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Applies to every SBA 7(a) loan for a startup or a complete change of ownership
eventCatalog.note: At least 10% equity injection on total project cost; a seller note may cover at most half of it and only on full standby for the loan term. On a $300,000 purchase project: $30,000 of own cash, at least $15,000 of it unborrowed.

eventCatalog.name: Sales tax is due on the equipment you bought
eventCatalog.text: Buying a business is also buying its chairs, fridges and machines. The state taxes that part of the price at 8.875%.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Allocation of the purchase price to tangible personal property in the contract
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Every asset purchase
eventCatalog.note: 8.875% x $40,000 allocated to furniture, fixtures and equipment (my allocation). Inventory for resale, goodwill and the lease are not taxed.

eventCatalog.name: Fourteen days with the disclosure document
eventCatalog.text: The franchisor may not take your signature or your money until you have had its disclosure document for 14 calendar days.
eventCatalog.realSignal: FTC Franchise Rule, 16 CFR Part 436
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Every franchise sale in the United States; New York also requires registration of the offering with the Attorney General
eventCatalog.note: The 14 days begin the day after delivery, so signing is possible on day 15 (FTC compliance guide).

eventCatalog.name: The royalty comes off the top
eventCatalog.text: Before rent, wages or milk, 8.5% of every sale goes to the franchisor: 6% royalty and 2.5% for marketing.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Item 6 of the franchise disclosure document
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Every month for the life of the agreement
eventCatalog.note: Gregorys Coffee: 6% + 2.5% = 8.5% ($4,335 a month at $51,000 of sales). Dunkin': 5.9% + 5% = 10.9% ($5,559). The independent reference shop nets $9,719 a month before owner taxes: the royalty takes 45-57% of that. Dunkin's 5.9% and 5% were read on the opened Inspire Brands page; the Gregorys figures are search extracts.

eventCatalog.name: The franchisor dictates the build-out
eventCatalog.text: The design, the equipment list and the suppliers are in the manual. The lean kit is not an option: you build what the brand specifies.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Item 7 (initial investment) and Item 8 (required suppliers) of the disclosure document
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Standard franchise terms
eventCatalog.note: Lowest disclosed investment against the pack's own lean path: Gregorys from $459,150 / $224,000 starting capital of the independent cafe = 2.05. Dunkin' from $443,000.

eventCatalog.name: The brand has never had a franchisee
eventCatalog.text: You would be among the first franchisees. The disclosure document has no track record of franchised shops: nobody to call, no closures to count.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Item 20 of the disclosure document (franchised outlets opened, transferred and closed)
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Gregorys Coffee, with 50+ company shops, launched its franchise program in February 2026
eventCatalog.note: The awareness effect is a design value. The real point is informational: the usual check of a franchise, calling existing franchisees, is impossible.

eventCatalog.name: The city releases 2,200 new cart licenses
eventCatalog.text: A new fiscal year starts and the Health Department offers 2,200 supervisory licenses to people on the waiting list. Only a current licensed vendor can be on it.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Health Department waiting-list offers under Local Law 18 of 2021 and Local Laws 54 and 59 of 2026 (2,200 a year, fiscal 2027-2031, from July 1, 2026)
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Yearly through fiscal 2031; about 5,100 existing permits; the waiting list held nearly 10,000 vendors in October 2023 (Independent Budget Office, cited by the Queens Eagle) and advocates speak of 20,000 or more
eventCatalog.note: With 10,000 to 20,000 waiting and 2,200 a year, a newcomer's place in line is 4.5 to 9 years away if nobody drops out: each yearly release moves the player 12 months closer. The city's business page gives a larger total (12,780 by 2031) than the per-year figure implies.

eventCatalog.name: Vending enforcement sweeps the corridor
eventCatalog.text: Sanitation enforcement officers and police work their way down the avenue checking licenses and decals. Vendors without them are ticketed and some carts are taken.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Complaints from storefront businesses and elected officials about a vending corridor; city enforcement operations
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Ongoing: "Ahead of New Law, Street Vendors Still Face NYPD Crackdowns" (Documented, March 2026); fines start at $1,000 for mobile food vendors
eventCatalog.note: $1,000 per summons (Health Department schedule). 7 days closed is my estimate for a seized cart. A licensed vendor with a valid decal is not affected.

eventCatalog.name: No commissary has a space for your cart
eventCatalog.text: Without a commissary agreement you cannot pass the pre-permit inspection, and the garages near your corner are full.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Capacity of Health Department-permitted commissaries
eventCatalog.realFrequency: A city report notes that vendors must store units in permitted commissaries "which have limited capacity"
eventCatalog.note: Design values: a month of searching and a dearer commissary further away ($900 instead of $600).

eventCatalog.name: Lattes change the class of your cart
eventCatalog.text: A cart that serves brewed coffee and tea is the simplest class. Add milk drinks that need refrigeration and the cart needs different equipment, a different class and a new inspection.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Menu of the cart against Health Code Chapter 6 unit classes
eventCatalog.realFrequency: A rule, not an incident
eventCatalog.note: Health Code Chapter 6, seen in extract: a Class D unit serves foods that need no temperature control, "such as brewed coffee and tea", and counts as non-processing ($75 permit). The $5,000 for refrigeration and a hand-wash setup and the 21 days for re-inspection are my estimates; which class a milk-based espresso menu falls in was not confirmed.

eventCatalog.name: The market season ends
eventCatalog.text: The open-air food markets close for the winter. A stand that lives on weekend crowds has nowhere to stand until April.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Operating calendar of the seasonal markets (Smorgasburg's 16th season opened in April 2026 at three sites)
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Every year
eventCatalog.note: April-to-October season assumed from the reported April opening; the exact closing date was not seen. The shared-corner option trades all year.

eventCatalog.name: A Health inspector walks the market
eventCatalog.text: The inspector asks every stand for its temporary permit number. A stand without one is closed on the spot.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Organizer's vendor list filed with the Health Department 30 days before the event; inspection at the event
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Stated by the Health Department: vendors without a valid permit face a summons of $200-$2,000 and immediate closing
eventCatalog.note: Base of the fine range used; the lost day is the event day.

eventCatalog.name: The host wants the corner back
eventCatalog.text: The shop that housed your coffee counter is changing its layout. You worked under its permit and its lease: you have 30 days to leave.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Terms of the written agreement with the host
eventCatalog.realFrequency: No statistic; follows from operating under another operator's permit and supervision
eventCatalog.note: Design values. Fires at the end of the agreed term unless the agreement gives a renewal right.

eventCatalog.name: The Parks Department asks for kiosk proposals
eventCatalog.text: A request for proposals is out for food kiosks in a park. Proposals are due in five weeks; the winner pays the city a guaranteed minimum or a share of sales, whichever is higher.
eventCatalog.realSignal: NYC Parks concession solicitations in the City Record (Battery kiosks: issued May 5, 2026, due June 12, 2026)

effects.note: example minimum fee of $40,000 a year, or 4% of gross if higher

eventCatalog.realFrequency: Several solicitations a year across the park system
eventCatalog.note: Page opened (City Record): a 2024 Parks award for a cafe at Dag Hammarskjold Park, with an option for one mobile food unit, sets the fee at the greater of a minimum or a share of gross: year 1 $40,000 vs 4%, then $42,000, $44,100 and $46,305. $40,000 / 12 = $3,333 a month. The five-week proposal window is from the 2026 Battery kiosks solicitation (search extract).

eventCatalog.name: The staff you kept arrive with sick days owed
eventCatalog.text: The baristas who stayed through the sale still hold the paid sick hours they earned under the old owner. They are yours to pay now.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Unused safe and sick leave balances of retained employees on the closing date
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Applies to every sale where staff stay: the city's rules say sales and transfers "shall not impact employees' protected time off balances"
eventCatalog.note: Worst case for four retained baristas with half of the yearly 40 hours unused: 4 x 20 hours x $21 = $1,680 over the year. The price can be reduced by the same amount if the review finds the balances. Denying the hours is the existing no_paid_sick_leave shortcut, with seller and buyer jointly liable.

eventCatalog.name: The landlord's contribution arrives after you have paid
eventCatalog.text: The lease promised a construction allowance. It is a reimbursement: the landlord pays after the work is finished, inspected and free of liens. Until then every invoice is on you.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Work letter terms: allowance paid on completion against lien waivers
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Standard structure where an allowance exists; small storefront tenants more often get free rent instead
eventCatalog.note: One NYC restaurant-lease source puts allowances at $50-$150 per sq ft for strong tenants (not confirmed elsewhere). The $20,000 is a design example: $25 per sq ft on 800 sq ft, far below that range, as a first-time tenant would get. A mechanic's lien on the job blocks the payout.

eventCatalog.name: Free permit help at the Buildings office
eventCatalog.text: The Department of Buildings holds free walk-in sessions for small business owners, and Small Business Services offers a project manager. Owners who use them get answers before they file, not after an objection.
eventCatalog.realSignal: DOB small-business sessions and NYC BEST enrollment
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Standing services; the July 2026 executive order expands them
eventCatalog.note: The 10% is a design value; the city has published no measured effect.

eventCatalog.name: The Certificate of Occupancy does not say "eating and drinking"
eventCatalog.text: The architect pulls the building's Certificate of Occupancy: the ground floor is listed as a store. A cafe there needs the Buildings Department to accept the use, or the owner to amend the certificate.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Use shown on the Certificate of Occupancy on file for the address (public record)
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Applies to every space that was not a food business before; the city lists it first among Buildings violations for restaurants, with a $400-$25,000 penalty
eventCatalog.note: Page opened: "If you plan to change the use, egress, or occupancy of your space, make sure the property owner has filed for an amended Certificate of Occupancy." One architecture firm says a store converted to an eating and drinking place for under 75 people can often proceed on a Letter of No Objection instead of an amended certificate (secondary, not confirmed with the Department). 30 days is the letter's wait in a clear case; an amended certificate takes far longer and no measured time was found.

eventCatalog.name: A neighbor complains about construction noise
eventCatalog.text: The tenant upstairs calls 311 about the demolition. An environmental inspector comes to look for the noise plan that every site must post.
eventCatalog.realSignal: 311 construction-noise complaint about the address

effects.note: only if no plan is posted

eventCatalog.realFrequency: Noise is among the most common 311 complaints in the city; no rate per site was found
eventCatalog.note: Page opened: "Construction sites must post a Construction Noise Plan... It must be visible at the site all the time... You do not need to file the plan with the Department of Environmental Protection"; not following the requirements can bring "significant financial penalties". The $440 is the lowest figure visible in a garbled search extract of the Noise Code penalty schedule (roughly $440 to $4,200 by offense): an unconfirmed estimate. After-hours work without a variance multiplies complaints. A site with its plan posted and its permits in order loses nothing.

mechanics.playerDecision: Which space to lease (former cafe, former food shop, raw space), how many free months to bargain for (lever free_rent_deal), whether rent starts at signing or at delivery and permits (lever lease_contingencies), and how fast to build (lever construction_pace).

Events of extra.eventCatalog add days to one track; only delays on the longest track move openingDay. Revenue is zero until openingDay.

mechanics.playerDecision: Pick a listing on the map; choose how deeply to check it (lever takeover_due_diligence); file or skip the bulk-sale notice; when to apply for permits (lever takeover_permit_timing); how to treat staff, menu and name in the first month (lever takeover_transition).

mechanics.title: What the guaranty costs on the day you give up
mechanics.playerDecision: Chosen at signing (lever guaranty_type); felt at closing or bankruptcy: give notice and keep paying, or walk away.

mechanics.title: Parallel tracks: the opening date is set by the longest one
mechanics.playerDecision: What to start early: apply for the Health permit three weeks before construction ends, order equipment at plan approval, file the utility request at lease signing, hire and train in the last two weeks. mechanics.engineMath: Each roadmap step has dependsOn[] and durationDays; the player presses "start" on any step whose dependencies are done. openingDay = the day the last required step finishes. The engine shows the critical path and, for each waiting day, the rent it burns. Steps that cannot: asbestos report before the DOB permit; DOB permit before construction; construction before trade inspections; Landmarks permit before the DOB permit.

nonObvious.text: The Health permit dies with the sale. A buyer who opens on Monday on the seller's permit is an unpermitted restaurant.
nonObvious.why: Health Code §5.11 voids a permit on any transfer; the buyer can apply 22 days before closing and lose no day, but only if someone tells them.

nonObvious.text: Buying a shop can make you personally liable for sales tax the seller never paid, up to the full price.
nonObvious.why: Tax Law §1141(c): without Form AU-196.10 filed 10 days before paying, the buyer inherits the debt whether or not money was held back.

nonObvious.text: You pay 8.875% sales tax on the chairs and machines when you buy a business.
nonObvious.why: A bulk sale is also a retail sale of tangible property; only inventory for resale, goodwill and the lease escape. The split of the price in the contract sets the bill.

nonObvious.text: The seller's unemployment-insurance record becomes yours.
nonObvious.why: The state moves the experience account to the buyer and recalculates the rate from the transfer date; not reporting the purchase does not stop it.

nonObvious.text: Staff who stay through a sale keep their unused sick leave, and buyer and seller are jointly liable for it.
nonObvious.why: City rule 6 RCNY §7-210: sales and transfers do not affect balances.

nonObvious.text: The city can refuse the buyer a permit because the seller left fines unpaid.
nonObvious.why: Health Code Article 5: no new permit on a sale where records show outstanding violations or unpaid penalties, unless the sale is proven arm's length.

nonObvious.text: The seller stays on the hook for the lease after selling.
nonObvious.why: An assignor remains liable on the rent covenant unless the landlord releases it, so sellers want strong buyers and landlords get two pockets.

nonObvious.text: A profitable cafe costs about twice its owner's yearly earnings, which is more than building the same room.
nonObvious.why: Sold US coffee shops: median 2.0 x earnings, 0.41 x sales. The pack's reference shop prices at about $233,000 against a $70,000 light build-out: the buyer pays for months of rent not burned and customers already won.

nonObvious.text: "Key money" buys a room, not a business.
nonObvious.why: The payment is for a lease and what is bolted down; it is worth it only if the inherited rent is below market with years left. A closed cafe's customers are gone.

nonObvious.text: The free-rent months are almost never enough.
nonObvious.why: Three to six free months against 8-12 months from signing to opening: the gap is paid rent with no income, and it is the single largest hidden cost of building.

nonObvious.text: A signed lease does not mean you have the space.
nonObvious.why: A holdover tenant or the landlord's unfinished work can delay delivery by months; courts found five months reasonable. Unless the lease ties rent to delivery, the clock runs.

nonObvious.text: A good guy guaranty protects you only if you leave by the book.
nonObvious.why: Written notice of 3-6 months, rent paid to the last day, keys back, room broom-clean. Skip a step and the guaranty can cover the rest of the term.

nonObvious.text: First-time owners are turned away from the best blocks.
nonObvious.why: Landlords with a choice of tenants pick operators with a record; a first shop often has to start in a second-tier location or by buying an existing lease.

nonObvious.text: Rent is not the rent: the lease adds the landlord's tax increases.
nonObvious.why: Tax escalation over a base year can add $10-$20 per sq ft a year in older buildings; a low base year turns a reassessment into the tenant's bill.

nonObvious.text: The deposit is often not cash but a bank letter of credit that takes weeks and locks up the same cash anyway.
nonObvious.why: Banks issue it against collateral, charge about 1-2% a year and need 2-3 weeks; the lease cannot be signed without it.

nonObvious.text: A sentence in the lease about who owns the improvements decides whether your build-out labor is taxed.
nonObvious.why: Tenant installations are presumed temporary and taxable; if title passes to the landlord, Form ST-124 makes the work a capital improvement.

nonObvious.text: You cannot get a Buildings permit in most New York storefronts without an asbestos report first.
nonObvious.why: Any building from before April 1987 needs an ACP-5 by a certified investigator before DOB issues a permit; a positive result adds abatement and a week of notice.

nonObvious.text: The landlord's unpaid city fines can block the tenant's permit.
nonObvious.why: Local Law 160 of 2017 denies permits on properties with large arrears; the tenant must document an exception.

nonObvious.text: Paint, floors and cabinets need no permit; moving a sink does.
nonObvious.why: DOB lists painting, plastering, cabinets and floor resurfacing as permit-free; plumbing beyond a fixture swap needs a licensed master plumber and usually filed plans. A truly cosmetic refresh of a former cafe can skip the whole permit track.

nonObvious.text: The penalty for building without a permit is a multiple of the fee you skipped: 21 times, at least $6,000.
nonObvious.why: Local Law 156 of 2017. On a $915 fee the formula gives $19,215, capped at $15,000, and the permit must still be obtained while the site sits under a Stop Work Order.

nonObvious.text: If a worker falls during your build-out, you, the tenant, can be sued as the "owner".
nonObvious.why: Labor Law §240 imposes absolute liability on owners, and courts apply it to the tenant who contracted for the work; this is why insured contractors cost more in New York.

nonObvious.text: Your contractor's unpaid subcontractor can put a lien on your landlord's building eight months later.
nonObvious.why: A lien is usually a lease default; removing it takes a bond of 110% of the claim. Lien waivers with each payment prevent it.

nonObvious.text: A coffee shop does not need gas, and choosing it can cost two months.
nonObvious.why: Restaurants waited an average of 68 days for gas service in the last survey; an all-electric cafe has no gas track at all.

nonObvious.text: The espresso machine, the ice machine and the air conditioner can exceed what the old panel carries.
nonObvious.why: A service upgrade needs Con Edison: weeks if the building has capacity, 6-24 months if the street side must be rebuilt.

nonObvious.text: A new business pays the utility a deposit of up to two months of bills.
nonObvious.why: No payment history; the amount is estimated from a similar business and can be challenged.

nonObvious.text: In a historic district the sign and the awning need a second agency's permit before the first.
nonObvious.why: Landmarks approval precedes the Buildings permit; staff approve complete applications in 10-15 business days, but an incomplete one is returned.

nonObvious.text: An old building may have no Certificate of Occupancy at all, and then the cafe needs a letter saying the use is legal.
nonObvious.why: Pre-1938 buildings: a Letter of No Objection from the borough office, at least a month, and a refusal kills the project after the lease is signed.

nonObvious.text: The Health Department sells a practice inspection for $100, but only after you have opened.
nonObvious.why: It is available between the first day of service and the first graded inspection; nothing found counts against the grade.

nonObvious.text: The 22 days to open count from the application, not from the end of construction.
nonObvious.why: The application needs insurance, the sales-tax certificate and a food protection course registration, not a finished room; applying early removes the wait.

nonObvious.text: The city now assigns a free project manager to anyone opening a business.
nonObvious.why: Executive Order 18 of July 2026: the NYC Business Express Service Team identifies permits, helps file and coordinates inspections.

nonObvious.text: A free lawyer will read your lease if you qualify.
nonObvious.why: Commercial Lease Assistance Program: 812 businesses in the year to June 2025; call-back within three business days.

nonObvious.text: One storefront in nine is empty, and that is the tenant's bargaining power.
nonObvious.why: 11.0% citywide vacancy in April 2026, 21.1% in the Financial District: landlords of long-empty stores give more free rent.

nonObvious.text: A franchise takes its cut before you pay rent.
nonObvious.why: Royalty plus marketing is 8.5% (Gregorys) to 10.9% (Dunkin') of sales, about half of what the independent reference shop earns before owner taxes.

nonObvious.text: Starbucks cannot be franchised, and a coffee franchise costs twice an independent shop.
nonObvious.why: Dunkin' from $443,000, Gregorys from $459,150, with liquidity and net-worth tests; the franchisor dictates design and suppliers.

nonObvious.text: A food cart permit costs $75, and you cannot get one.
nonObvious.why: New year-round permits go only to supervisory-license holders from a waiting list of 10,000 to 20,000; 2,200 a year are released through 2031.

nonObvious.text: A cart on private property needs no place in the queue.
nonObvious.why: A Restricted Area permit has no waiting list and no cap, but the sidewalk in front of the property is public and off limits.

nonObvious.text: Every cart needs a garage with a Health Department permit, visited daily.
nonObvious.why: No commissary agreement, no permit; capacity is limited and prices are not published.

nonObvious.text: A brewed-coffee cart is the simplest class; milk drinks can change the class of the cart.
nonObvious.why: Health Code Chapter 6 puts carts serving foods that need no temperature control, "such as brewed coffee and tea", in the non-processing class.

nonObvious.text: A corner in someone else's shop has no permit of its own.
nonObvious.why: The city describes renting space in a permitted restaurant under its operator's supervision; the host carries the inspection and can end the arrangement.

nonObvious.text: A park kiosk is won in a public bid and pays the city a minimum or a share of sales, whichever is more.
nonObvious.why: Parks concessions run through requests for proposals with five-week windows and multi-year terms.

nonObvious.text: To borrow from the SBA to buy a shop you need a tenth of the project in your own cash.
nonObvious.why: SOP 50 10 8 (2025): 10% equity injection; a seller note counts for half of it at most and only if the seller waits out the loan.

nonObvious.text: Imported espresso machines carry a 15% tariff; a used machine already in the country does not.
nonObvious.why: US tariff on EU goods since July 2025; buying a shop with its equipment sidesteps it.

nonObvious.text: A cafe renovation must have a noise plan taped up on site, and nobody tells you because it is not filed anywhere.
nonObvious.why: The Construction Noise Mitigation Plan is posted, not submitted; its absence turns a neighbor's 311 call into a fine.

nonObvious.text: Only the building's owner can amend the Certificate of Occupancy, and the tenant pays the fine if the use is wrong.
nonObvious.why: Occupancy contrary to the certificate is fined $400-$25,000; the city tells tenants to make sure the owner has filed, which means making it a condition of the lease.

nonObvious.text: The city publishes its fines for restaurants on one page, by agency, with the amounts.
nonObvious.why: The NYC Business restaurant page lists penalties from $5 (no carter decal) to $25,000 (wrong occupancy) and can be opened without trouble: a ready primary source for the other researchers' violations.

failureStories.what: Artisanal Fromagerie Bistro leased 387 Park Avenue South and never opened the restaurant; a judge ruled it owed the landlord more than $24 million in rent.
failureStories.cause: Long lease signed, build-out never completed, two bankruptcy filings dismissed.
failureStories.lesson: Rent runs from the lease, not from the opening; the lease can outweigh everything else the business owns.

failureStories.what: The relaunched Le Figaro Cafe in Greenwich Village sued its landlord in 2022 claiming about $2 million in losses.
failureStories.cause: Months of construction-permit delays, then contractors stopped when they uncovered a buckling interior wall.
failureStories.lesson: Structure hidden in an old building can stop a job for months; the lease must say who pays and whether rent runs.

failureStories.what: Papaya King's owner spent $500,000 on a new space and could not open there.
failureStories.cause: A ventilation problem made the space unusable; a lockout dispute with the landlord followed.
failureStories.lesson: Check ventilation and what the building allows before spending on a space.

failureStories.what: Bocca di Bacco walked away from a signed Upper West Side lease and about $100,000 in 2014.
failureStories.cause: City approvals dragged on; the owners blamed red tape.
failureStories.lesson: Make the lease conditional on permits, or the deposit and the first months are lost.

failureStories.what: A Bronx small-business owner paid rent for 15 months before opening.
failureStories.cause: Permit and approval delays while the lease clock ran.
failureStories.lesson: Budget paid rent before the first sale in months, not weeks.

failureStories.what: A Lower East Side restaurant opened with salads and cold tapas in 2015.
failureStories.cause: Con Edison took seven months to turn on its gas.
failureStories.lesson: A menu that needs gas waits for the utility; a menu that does not opens on time.

failureStories.what: An East Village deli at 75 Second Avenue sat finished but closed for months in 2022.
failureStories.cause: A Fire Department certificate of approval stuck in review; partners said they could not keep paying bills from their own pockets.
failureStories.lesson: One missing sign-off holds the whole opening; start every agency track at lease signing.

failureStories.what: Cafe Peanut in Jersey City could not open ten months after signing its lease.
failureStories.cause: The owners said the landlord's renovations were shoddy and the space was not ready when promised.
failureStories.lesson: Landlord's work needs a delivery date with consequences in the lease.

failureStories.what: The founder of White Noise Coffee could not rent even 200-300 sq ft in a trendy New York neighborhood.
failureStories.cause: Landlords would not take a first-time operator.
failureStories.lesson: She converted her parents' bodega instead and now runs three shops: a second-tier address you control beats a prime one you cannot get.

failureStories.what: Buyers of delis and restaurants were assessed for their sellers' sales tax in a line of New York Tax Appeals cases.
failureStories.cause: No bulk-sale notice, or a late one.
failureStories.lesson: File Form AU-196.10 ten days before paying and keep the price in escrow until the state answers.

failureStories.what: A Junction Boulevard fruit vendor pays up to $25,000 every two years to rent a cart permit that costs its holder $200.
failureStories.cause: The cap on permits and a waiting list of about 10,000.
failureStories.lesson: The cheap way into food vending is cheap only for those who already hold a permit.

failureStories.what: A Hell's Kitchen restaurant cooked without gas for about six weeks in spring 2026.
failureStories.cause: A routine utility inspection found a leak in the building's piping; landlord's plumber and utility each waited for the other.
failureStories.lesson: Gas in an old building is a shared pipe you do not control.
